analysis.one_liner: Requires groups that spend on elections to disclose donors of $10,000 or more.
analysis.headline: The bill sat without action after its April 2019 referral to the Senate Rules Committee, receiving no hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require corporations, unions, Super PACs, and tax-exempt groups that spend money to influence federal elections to file reports naming anyone who gave them $10,000 or more, and to name the people who actually own or control them. It would extend the existing ban on foreign money in elections to paid internet ads and ballot initiatives, require CEOs to certify under oath that foreign nationals did not shape their political spending, and require political ads to carry a statement identifying the group's top funders, similar to the 'I approve this message' line for candidates.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who see campaign ads but cannot currently find out who is bankrolling them. Today, Super PACs and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups can raise unlimited sums and spend on elections without ever naming their donors; this bill would force those names into public, searchable filings within 24 hours of spending. It would also tighten rules aimed at keeping foreign money out of elections.

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations spending more than $10,000 on election-related activity must file a report under penalty of perjury within 24 hours of each disclosure date, naming anyone who gave them $10,000 or more during the cycle.
Non-publicly-traded corporations and other covered entities must list their beneficial owners — the real people who control them — so political spending cannot be routed through shell companies.

The bill expands the foreign-money ban: foreign nationals could no longer take part in decisions about election spending, contribute to state or local ballot initiatives and referenda, or pay for online and digital political ads, and the Federal Election Commission would audit each election cycle for illicit foreign money.

Political ads not authorized by candidates would have to carry a statement naming the group's top funders — the five largest for video ads, two for audio — in place of or alongside the standard disclaimer.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, Super PACs, tax-exempt political groups, and labor unions that would face new reporting duties: filing disclosure statements naming large donors, listing beneficial owners, CEO certifications on foreign involvement, and funder lists on their ads. Lobbyists and consultants whose value depends on keeping funders anonymous would lose that product.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark money groups and big spenders

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden is real: any covered organization crossing $10,000 in election-related spending must file detailed reports within 24 hours, and groups that mix commercial activity with political activity would need to sort every payment between the two, a compliance cost that falls heaviest on smaller organizations.

Publicly naming large donors of both parties raises the risk that some givers face threats or harassment; the bill responds with an exception for people facing serious threats, harassment, or reprisals, but critics could argue the exception is inconsistent and the exposure itself is a cost.

The bill relies on the Federal Election Commission to write rules, audit foreign money, and enforce the requirements, and the FEC has often operated without a quorum or with divided commissioners, which could slow or hollow out enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: voters gain a public record of who is financing election ads, and the biggest political spenders gain new reporting duties and lose anonymity. The harassment risk and compliance load are genuine but the bill addresses the first with exceptions and targets disclosure at $10,000-plus givers rather than small donors. The main practical weakness is enforcement, which depends on an FEC with a poor track record of functioning. On balance this is a transparency bill whose costs fall on the organizations being asked to disclose, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on April 11, 2019, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, with 44 Democratic and independent cosponsors.
The bill's only action was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration; the committee took no further action and the full Senate never considered it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Organizations that spend large sums on elections without naming their donors — corporations, Super PACs, and tax-exempt 'dark money' groups — are better off, since the disclosure requirements never took effect. Senate leaders who preferred not to bring the bill to a vote are also better off, having avoided a recorded position.

against.name: Sen. Roy Blunt
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 116th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought campaign-finance disclosure legislation to the Senate floor during the 116th Congress, and campaigned against disclosure requirements for political spending as unconstitutional restrictions on speech.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, none was a Republican, and the bill sat in committee in a Senate run by Republicans, so it never drew a vote to measure the split.

industries.industry: Super PACs and 'dark money' tax-exempt groups
industries.note: These groups raise unlimited money for elections without naming donors; the bill would force them to file reports naming every $10,000-plus giver within 24 hours and would treat transfers between allied groups as covered. Their business model depends on the anonymity the bill removes, which is why their loss is the voter's gain.

Non-publicly-traded companies spending on elections would have to list their beneficial owners and have their CEOs certify under penalty of perjury that no foreign national directed their political spending. This closes the shell-company route to anonymous election spending.

Labor organizations are covered organizations under the bill and would face the same donor-disclosure and ad-funder rules as corporations. Unions have historically opposed disclosure mandates, saying members face harassment, though the bill includes a harassment exception and treats ordinary member dues as commercial transactions excluded from reporting.

industries.industry: Political advertising and digital media platforms
industries.note: The bill extends the foreign-money ban to paid internet and digital political ads and requires funder lists and disclaimers on streamed, audio, and prerecorded-call political ads. Platforms and broadcasters would carry slightly longer ad disclaimers but the main change is that political ads become traceable to their funders.
